newsitem.title: UK: LME aluminium erodes further, others see losses.
newsitem.headline: LME aluminium erodes further, others see losses.

text.p: Aluminium lurched lower on Monday afternoon to its lowest levels in nearly 2-1/2 years, compounding earlier losses, and most of the other metals joined it in the minus column.
Aluminium crumbled to a fresh nadir earlier and briefly stabilised after lunch. But fresh selling hit prices, sending them to a low of $1,332 a tonne, the weakest since May 1994.
Last kerb business was done at $1,336, down $21 from Friday's kerb close.
Bounces were not ruled out in the short-term, but most players expected further downside moves eventually.
"Short covering rallies remain a possibility but chart counts to the $1,315 region are still readable," broker Gerald said.
Copper also got the wind knocked out when a prominent trader made some bearish forecasts.
Prices had already come off session highs of $1,929 in the morning, but they slid further to a low of $1,900 after a speech by Herbert Black, president of American Iron and Metal Co Inc.
Black, a scrap merchant widely believed to be among those repsonsible for breaking Sumitomo's grasp on the copper market, said Sumitomo may not have liquidated all of its long positions.
"The dip in prices has to be something to do with this. These comments are not going to help at all," said one trader.
Prices closed on the afternoon kerb at $1,905, down $6.

Black also told a luncheon the copper price may shoot higher in the short-term before scoring more losses, slumping to $1,600 next year and $1,400 in 1998. The market would see a sustained contango by November or the beginning of the New Year, he added.
On Monday morning the cash/threes backwardation widened, but ended the day slightly narrower at $3/$8.
LME inventories were expected to fall again on Tuesday after stocks dropped by a healthy 9,925 tonnes on Friday.
Most of the other metals joined copper and aluminium in the weaker trend.
Nickel shed $140 to $7,030, only $20 off its low, after receiving a boost from a stock drawdown on Friday.
Next support is pegged at $6,970, chartists said.
Tin settled at its low of $6,020 after losing $75. The next floor was expected to come in around $5,970, near the October 2 low, then $5,900, the previous day's nadir.
Lead edged down to $767, off $4 and zinc bucked the trend and finished $1 higher at $1,025.
Alloy finished weaker at $1,205 after Friday's close of $1,210/15.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8065
